Godāvarī
(‘the best of the givers of water’)
------------------------------------------
Even today, a devout and orthodox Hindu, invokes seven sacred rivers of India at the time of bath and also during the ritualistic worship of the family deity. गोदावरी is one of them. Gautamī and Vṛddhagaṅgā are two other names for it, though less known.
The invocation runs like this:
gaṅge ca yamune caiva
godāvari sarasvati ।
narmade सिन्धु kāveri
jale’smin sannidhiṁ कुरु ॥
“Oh गङ्गा! यमुना! गोदावरी! सरस्वती! नर्मदा! Sindhū! कावेरी! Please be present in this water here!”
The water can be the one used for one’s bath or for worshipping the deity.
गोदावरी">River GodāvarīUnlike the rivers सरस्वती and गङ्गा, the name of गोदावरी has not been mentioned in the Vedic literature. However there are enough references to it in the two epics and the पुराणस्. In importance and sacredness, it has been given a status next only to that of गङ्गा. In fact the Brahmapurāṇa (78.77) goes to the extent of declaring that the गङ्गा to the south of the विन्ध्य mountains is Gautamī (Godāvarī).
The river originates from the Brahmagiri hill near Tryambakeśvar in the Nasik district of Maharashtra State. It flows towards the east and joins the Bay of Bengal near Rājamahendram (or Rajamundry) where it is almost 6.4 kms. (4 miles) wide. It then divides itself into two branches Gautamī गोदावरी and वसिष्ठ गोदावरी. The latter again branches off into Vainateya गोदावरी.
The total length of the river is 1465 kms. (915 miles). It is joined by a few important tributaries like Pūrṇā, Phenagaṅgā, Vardhā, Vainagaṅgā, Prāṇahitā, Indrāvatī and शबरी.
There ia an interesting legend in the पुराणस् according to which the sage गौतम, the husband of अहल्या, brought this river (originally the गङ्गा) from the matted locks of शिव, to this earth, near Brahmagiri. At his request, शिव also agreed to stay near his hermitage. This became the famous त्र्यम्बकेश्वर.
According to the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, Śrī राम lived in the पञ्चवटी on the bank of the river गोदावरी, during his sojourn in the दण्डक forest. It was from here that सीता was abducted by the demon-king रावण.
A bath in the गोदावरी, especially during its पुष्कर-period (when the planet बृहस्पति or गुरु or जुपितेर् enters the zodiacal sign Siṁha or Leo) is considered extremely holy. The पुष्कर-period comes once in twelve years and lasts for 12 days.
Śrāddhas and tarpaṇas offered to the manes during the period, will save them from हेल्ल् and may even give them लिबेरतिओन्.
The holy places, of पिल्ग्रिमगे, situated on the banks of the गोदावरी are: गोवर्धन, जनस्थान, नासिक् and पञ्चवटी. There are several temples in these places. For the pilgrims who visit नासिक्, a bath in the Rāmakuṇḍa, on the left bank of गोदावरी, is a must.
The famous temple of राम at भद्राचलम् in the Khammam district of Andhra Pradesh is another holy place on the गोदावरी, frequented by the devotees.

godāna
(‘gifting of a cow’)
------------------------------------------
See COW.
‘Godāna’ is also the name of a saṁskāra or sacrament wherein the hair on the head (go = hair) above the right ear is shaved off. ‘Keśānta’ is another name for it.
See KEŚĀNTA for details.

God
------------------------------------------
In हिन्दुइस्म्, God has been described by various terms such as भगवान् (possessor of blessed qualities and power), Dhātā (the Supporter and the Sustainer of the world), ईश्वर (the Lord), पर-mātman (the Supreme Self), परमेश्वर (the Supreme Lord), Vidhātā (the Creator) and so on.
Unlike the Semitic religions, हिन्दुइस्म् does not depend upon a single scripture. However, the entire body of its philosophical literature accepts the उपनिषद्स् and, to a great extent, the Bhagavadgītā, as authoritative and does not go against them. Hence any concept of God based on these books is welcome to practically all sections of हिन्दुइस्म्.
While deriving the concept of God, it is but natural for man to start from the world in which he lives and moves. So, the God of हिन्दुइस्म्, when looked at from this angle, is the Creator. However, he creates the entire world, not out of nothing which is illogical, but out of himself. After च्रेअतिओन्, he sustains it with his power, rules over it like an all-powerful emperor, meting out justice, as reward and punishment, in accordance with the deeds of the individual beings. At the end of one cycle of creation—Hinduism advocates the cyclic theory of creation—he withdraws the entire world order into himself.
The Hindu scriptures are eloquent while describing the qualities of God. He is all-knowing and all-powerful. He is the very personification of justice, love and beauty. In fact, he is the personification of all the blessed qualities that man can ever conceive of. He is ever ready to shower his grace, mercy and blessings on his च्रेअतिओन्. Really speaking, the very purpose of his creating this world is to shower his blessings on the creatures, to lead them gradually from less perfect states to more perfect ones. He is easily pleased by the prayers and supplication of his devotees. However his response to these prayers is guided by the principle, that it should not be in conflict with the cosmic law concerning the general welfare of the world, and the law of कर्म concerning the welfare of the particular individual.
The Hindu concept of God has two special features. Depending upon the needs and tastes of his votaries, he can appear to them in any form they like to worship, and respond through that form. He can also incarnate himself amongst human beings in order to lead them to his own kingdom. And this incarnating is a continuing process, taking place whenever and wherever he deems it necessary.
Then, there is the other, the imperso-nal, aspect of God, as the Absolute. ‘Brahman’ is the name usually given to this aspect. It means what is infinitely big. It is the Infinite itself. It transcends everything that is created. Yet it is so unlike anything we know that it defies all description. It has been stated that the only way by which it can be predicated, is the negative way: ‘Not this! Not this!’
In its own essential nature, it is defined as ‘Sat-cit-आनन्द,’ ‘existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss’. It is the basis or substratum of all existence, चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and joy.
Metaphysics points towards ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute. A thinking मिन्द् and a feeling heart—that is what a human being is—can accept only God, the Creator and the Ruler (Īśvara), since the world is very much a reality to it. The correlation between the ब्रह्मन् and this ईश्वर, though instinctively felt by the feeling heart, will ever remain an enigma to the thinking मिन्द्! Could this be due to the mysterious power of māyā?
